summary: Eno Reyes opens by situating Factory's mission in the transition from human-driven to agent-driven software development. He critiques the current zeitgeist of sprinkling AI onto decades-old human-centric tools, likening it to asking for faster horses rather than inventing the automobile. The core thesis is that organizations must delegate the majority of tasks across the entire SDLC to agents, which requires a platform with intuitive delegation interfaces, centralized context, reliable agent outputs, and infrastructure supporting thousands of parallel agents. Reyes shows a demo of a droid ingesting a task, grounding itself by searching the codebase, checking git branches, reviewing recent changes and organizational memories, then returning a plan with clarifying questions before executing, running pre-commit hooks, linting, and generating a CI-passing PR. He identifies context deficiency—not model capability—as the primary failure mode across thousands of analyzed sessions, urging engineers to feed agents the implicit context from standups, whiteboards, and meetings. On planning, he describes droids researching model releases, integrating product goals from organizational memory and design docs, and producing exportable plans. He shares Factory's own workflow of transcribing all meetings, combining notes with architecture context, and using a knowledge droid to surface patterns and constraints before iterating on a PRD that becomes a roadmap with parallelizable tickets. Reyes frames documentation as a knowledge base and map for droids to imitate team thinking. He then covers SRE applications, showing a droid converting a Sentry incident into an RCA and mitigation plan by pulling context from logs, runbooks, Slack, and past incidents, condensing hours of search into minutes. He explains that agent-native incident response becomes a learning cycle: teams cut response time in half, droids proactively suggest fixes for repeat incidents, and new engineers can query droids for team practices. This enables a shift from reactive to predictive operations. Reyes closes by emphasizing that agents amplify rather than replace engineers, with the best developers moving from the inner loop of writing code to the outer loop of managing agent systems. He argues the skill that matters most is clear thinking and effective communication with both humans and AI. He concludes with enterprise considerations around security, auditability, ownership, and indemnification, warning against running agents in yolo mode within enterprises.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The industry is transitioning from human-driven to agent-driven software development, but current tools are still human-centric with AI layered on top.
AI tools fail most often due to missing context, not insufficient model intelligence; providing implicit organizational context is the key unlock.
Factory's droids handle the full SDLC—planning, coding, testing, and incident response—not just code generation.
Organizational documentation and processes become a knowledge base that agents use to learn and imitate how a team thinks.
Agent-native incident response creates a learning cycle: cutting response time in half, reducing repeat incidents, and enabling new engineers to query droids for team practices.
The best developers are shifting from the inner loop of writing code to the outer loop of managing agent systems and patterns.
The most valuable future skill is clear thinking and effective communication with both humans and AI, not technical optimization of specific systems.
Enterprise adoption requires addressing security, audit logs, ownership, auditability, and indemnification—yolo mode is not acceptable for organizations.
Agents are amplifiers of developer capability, not replacements; the future belongs to developers who understand how to work with agents.
Understand the distinction between human-centric tools with AI layered on top versus agent-native development.

sections.title: Introduction and Vision for Agent-Driven Development
sections.summary: Eno Reyes introduces himself and Factory's thesis: the field is transitioning from human-driven to agent-driven development. He critiques the current approach of layering AI onto decades-old human-centric tools and argues that true power comes only when teams delegate the majority of SDLC tasks to agents, which requires a platform with delegation interfaces, centralized context, reliable outputs, and parallel agent infrastructure.

sections.title: Droid Demo: Task Delegation and Code Execution
sections.summary: Reyes shows a video of a droid receiving a task, grounding itself by searching the codebase, checking git branches, reviewing recent changes and organizational memories, then returning a plan with clarifying questions. After user input, the droid executes, writes code, runs pre-commit hooks and linters, and generates a CI-passing PR.

sections.title: Context as the Fundamental Bottleneck
sections.summary: Reyes argues AI tools are only as good as the context they receive. After analyzing thousands of sessions, Factory found failures stem from missing context, not inadequate models. He urges engineers to capture implicit context from standups, meetings, and whiteboards, and to think of AI as something between a coworker and a platform.

sections.title: Planning and Design with AI Agents
sections.summary: Reyes demonstrates droids assisting with planning: researching new model releases, leveraging internet search, codebase knowledge, product goals from organizational memory, and design docs. He describes Factory's own workflow of transcribing all meetings, combining notes with architecture context, and using a knowledge droid to surface patterns and constraints before iterating on a PRD that decomposes into a roadmap of parallelizable tickets.

sections.title: Documentation as Organizational Knowledge Base
sections.summary: Reyes reframes organizational documentation—PRDs, design docs, RCA templates, roadmaps, meeting transcriptions—as a knowledge base and map for droids to learn and imitate team thinking. Communicating the 'why' behind decisions provides context for both future developers and AI systems, yielding significant improvements in agent performance.

sections.title: Agent-Driven Incident Response and SRE
sections.summary: Reyes addresses incident response, showing a droid converting a Sentry incident into a full RCA and mitigation plan. Agents pull context from logs, past incidents, runbooks, and Slack, condensing hours of search into minutes. With organizational memory, agents build models of team response patterns, generate new runbooks, and update workflows automatically.

sections.title: Agent-Native Learning Cycles and Enterprise Considerations
sections.summary: Reyes explains that agent-native incident response becomes a learning cycle: teams cut response time in half, droids proactively suggest fixes after repeat incidents, and new engineers can query droids for team practices. This enables a shift from reactive to predictive operations. He emphasizes that agents amplify rather than replace engineers, with the best developers moving from the inner loop of writing code to the outer loop of managing agent systems. He argues the most valuable skill is clear thinking and effective communication with both humans and AI. He closes with enterprise considerations—security, audit logs, ownership, auditability, and indemnification—warning against yolo mode in enterprises, and offers attendees 20 million free tokens to try the platform.

demonstrations: Video demo of a droid ingesting a task, grounding in the codebase, proposing a plan with clarifying questions, then executing to produce a CI-passing PR.

Droid tasked with finding up-to-date information about a new model release and integrating it into an existing chat application, leveraging internet search, codebase knowledge, organizational memory, and design docs.
Droid converting a Sentry incident into a full RCA and mitigation plan by pulling context from system logs, past incidents, runbooks in Notion/Confluence, and Slack discussions.
limitations: Vibe coding does not work for legacy enterprise systems like a Java 7 app handling global bank transactions.
MCP requires individual developers to install servers, click through configurations, and manage API keys, which is not ideal.
Fully automating all of SRE and RCA work is not realistic today.
Better models reduce context failures but do not solve the root problem of missing context.
Current publicly available agent tools are incremental improvements rather than step-function changes.
Factory's mobile experience is not yet optimized.
Running agents in yolo mode is not acceptable for enterprise environments.
quantitativeClaims: Factory analyzed thousands of droid-assisted development sessions.
Factory transcribes every single interaction and meeting.

Teams using Factory cut incident response time in half.
